tagline: Graded dirt roads meet wilderness and an older wagon route in the Sierra.
intro: The Chimney Peak Backcountry Byway leaves Route 178 at Canebrake for the southern Sierra Nevada. Canebrake Road is graded dirt; the surrounding wilderness has rocky slopes, pinyon pine and sagebrush. The route belongs to the Bureau of Land Management’s backcountry-byway program, which designates secondary roads for automobile tours through or near scenic public lands. The Bureau of Land Management emphasizes primitive recreation and solitude in this rugged mountain country. Within Chimney Peak Wilderness, springs and streams interrupt the pine and sagebrush terrain, and wildflowers appear seasonally.

An older route crosses the wilderness: the Sacatar Trail, a wagon road into the Owens Valley once used by soldiers and cattlemen. The BLM’s byway program began in 1989, before the wilderness designation. The California Desert Protection Act created Chimney Peak Wilderness in 1994. The motor route runs beside part of that protected land.

Driving north from Route 178, you pass Domelands Wilderness on the left and Owens Peak Wilderness on the right. Approximately nine miles along Canebrake Road, the Long Valley/Chimney Basin junction divides the approach. The right fork continues toward Chimney Creek Campground; the left leads toward Long Valley Campground. The byway circles Chimney Peak and returns to Canebrake Road at Lamont Meadow.

moments.title: Canebrake
moments.text: Canebrake marks the byway’s departure from Route 178 into the southern Sierra Nevada. The community lies in the South Fork Valley, beside the creek that the highway follows down from Walker Pass. The creek joins the South Fork Kern River at Bloomfield Ranch, part of the Canebrake Ecological Reserve. The original townsite was about three miles farther east on Isabella-Walker Pass Road. Robert S. Williamson named Canebrake Creek in the fall of 1853 after a canebrake, or patch of bulrushes. The creek’s name thus describes a plant feature of the place.

moments.title: Chimney Creek Campground
moments.text: The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail crosses Canebrake Road just south of Chimney Creek Campground. The campground occupies an exclusion from Owens Peak Wilderness, with 36 sites beside Chimney Creek at 5,700 feet. Pinyon pines, grey pines and oaks grow along the creek. A separate primitive path, Chimney Creek Trail, begins at a cattle guard half a mile from the start of the campground road. The campground road branches into spurs serving the sites. The Pacific Crest crossing is on Canebrake Road itself, just south of the campground and its spurs.

moments.title: Long Valley
moments.text: Long Valley Campground occupies an exclusion from Domelands Wilderness. Its 13 primitive sites lead to a trail connection with the South Fork of the Kern River. The Volpe Trail begins near site 13 at the end of the campground road and runs three miles into the wilderness. That route is unmaintained.

practical: Long Valley: The two-mile campground access road typically requires a high-clearance 4x4. A BLM notice dated July 17, 2024 announced Long Valley Campground’s closure for wildland fire danger. (checked 2026-10-11)
